sysd-blocks-046.title: Database constraints: rules the data must satisfy
sysd-blocks-046.text: The string "ABC" is not an integer but 123 is, and a database can enforce exactly that distinction. Constraints are rules that restrict the data that can be stored in the relations of a database. They are usually expressions that return true or false for whether the data satisfies them. A constraint can apply to a single attribute, a tuple (a row), or an entire relation (a table). A domain, the set of possible values for an attribute, is itself a constraint. It can be narrowed further, such as limiting an integer attribute to values between 1 and 10. SQL does this with check constraints.

sysd-blocks-048.title: Relational operations: selection, projection and join
sysd-blocks-048.text: Codd's original relational algebra had eight operators in two groups of four. Queries on a relational database are expressed in relational calculus or relational algebra. Four operators come from set theory: union, intersection, set difference, and the cartesian product, which matches every tuple of one relation with every tuple of the other. The other four are selection (SELECT with a WHERE clause), projection (extracting only specified attributes), join (connecting relations by their common attributes) and division. In SQL an INNER JOIN prevents a cartesian product, so a query over N tables needs N-1 inner joins.

sysd-blocks-067.title: Handling relational data in NoSQL without joins
sysd-blocks-067.text:
Most NoSQL databases cannot join data in queries, so the schema generally needs to be designed differently. There are three main techniques for handling relational data.

The first is multiple queries: instead of one query, run several. NoSQL queries are often faster than SQL queries, so the cost may be acceptable, but if too many are needed another approach is more appropriate.

The second is non-normalized data. Instead of storing only foreign keys, store the actual foreign values with the data, such as a username in each blog comment, so no further lookup is needed. Copied values must be changed in many places when they change, so this approach works better when reads are much more common than writes.

The third is nesting data. In document databases like MongoDB, put more data in fewer collections. Blog comments can sit inside the post document, so one retrieval returns all the data a task needs.

sysd-blocks-047.title: Stored procedure: code that lives in the database
sysd-blocks-047.text: Some of an application's logic can live inside the database itself. A stored procedure is executable code that is associated with, and generally stored in, the database. It collects and customizes common operations, such as inserting a tuple into a relation, gathering usage statistics, or encapsulating complex business logic and calculations. Procedures can greatly reduce the information transferred within and outside a system. Access can also be granted only to the procedures and not directly to the tables, for added security. They are not part of the relational model, but all commercial implementations include them, often with vendor-specific procedural extensions to SQL.

sysd-blocks-050.title: Views and materialized views: computed relations
sysd-blocks-050.text: A view stores no data at all. Relations that store data are called base relations, and in implementations they are tables. Derived relations are computed by applying relational operations to other relations, and in implementations they are called views or queries. A materialized view goes the other way: it is a pre-computed data set derived from a query and stored for later use. Querying it is faster than querying the base table, significantly so for frequent or complex queries. Materialized views also enable data subsetting, which reduces network loads, and are mostly used for performance and for keeping copies.

sysd-blocks-174.title: Vector database: finding what is similar
sysd-blocks-174.text: Traditional databases look up records by exact match. A vector database finds records that are semantically similar to an input. It stores and retrieves embeddings, which are machine-learned vectors with a few hundred to tens of thousands of dimensions. Semantically similar items, whether words, documents, images or audio, get vectors close to each other. It typically uses approximate nearest neighbor algorithms, and uses include semantic search and recommendation engines. In retrieval-augmented generation, the prompt's embedding queries the database for relevant documents, which are added to the language model's context window.

sysd-blocks-053.title: Choosing a database by workload
sysd-blocks-053.text: No database is best at everything, so pick the kind that matches the workload. OLTP databases suit transactional systems requiring strong consistency, and OLAP databases are optimized for complex queries and data analysis. Full-text search databases give fast, flexible text search. Document stores hold and query JSON-like documents, and key-value stores offer high-speed, simple data models. Graph databases manage highly connected data. Vector databases store and retrieve vector representations efficiently, and geospatial databases specialize in location-based data and queries. Singh advises weighing both the ACID and BASE models, and the application's own requirements, when choosing.

sysd-blocks-164.title: Polyglot persistence: several databases in one system
sysd-blocks-164.text: Force one database to meet every requirement and the result can be a non-performant jack-of-all-trades, master of none, because different databases solve different problems. Polyglot persistence means using multiple data storage technologies within a single system to meet varying storage needs. The idea mirrors polyglot programming. As the right language for each job may beat one language for everything, an application can talk to several databases and use each for what it does best. Joins enforce relationships in a relational database but become problematic as data grows. A graph database may handle relationships at scale but not transactions, which relational systems serve better, and a document database can hold the unstructured part. Martin Fowler expects any decent-sized enterprise to use varied storage technologies for different kinds of data. He would first ask how the data will be manipulated and only then choose the technology. The approach has two major drawbacks: a significant increase in operational complexity, and no support for keeping data consistent across the separate stores.

sysd-blocks-056.title: BASE consistency model: looser than ACID
sysd-blocks-056.text: ACID promises a lot, and some databases deliberately promise less. BASE is a looser alternative that NoSQL databases often adopt to gain scale and resilience. It is built on three ideas: basic availability, soft state and a delayed kind of consistency. Its properties are much looser than ACID guarantees, and there is no direct one-for-one mapping between the two models. Basic availability means the database appears to work most of the time. Soft state means stores need not be write-consistent, nor replicas mutually consistent, all the time. The third idea, covered in {{ref:sysd-scale-097}}, is that data may not be consistent immediately but eventually becomes consistent. In the meantime reads remain possible but may give an incorrect response. To scale and stay highly available, the logic moves from the database to separate servers, so the database becomes more independent and focused on storing data.

sysd-blocks-057.title: ACID vs BASE: choosing by requirements
sysd-blocks-057.text:
Singh says there is no right answer between ACID and BASE. Both models were designed to satisfy different requirements, so choosing a database means weighing both against the application's needs.

A fully ACID database is the perfect fit where data reliability and consistency are essential. It fails the whole transaction if any step errors. Databases built around traditional ACID guarantees, such as relational ones, choose consistency over availability. SQL databases such as MySQL and PostgreSQL are structured over the ACID model.

BASE systems, common in NoSQL, choose availability over consistency, though MongoDB and Redis keep consistency and compromise availability when the network splits. A BASE database lets users read inconsistent data temporarily and reaches consistency later. DynamoDB and ElasticSearch use the BASE architecture. Developers must then be more rigorous about consistent data and know the chosen database's BASE behavior. Planning around BASE limitations can be a major disadvantage compared with the simplicity of ACID transactions. A database leans toward one side, though some NoSQL databases show certain ACID traits.

sysd-blocks-172.title: Time series database: built for timestamped data
sysd-blocks-172.text: Early time series databases were data historians recording sensor measurements. Today they also track the health of infrastructure and applications and serve IoT telemetry, smart energy grids and financial tick data. A time series database is optimized for data that forms a sequence of points indexed in chronological order. The data is uniform, timestamps mapped to metric values, and it grows rapidly. Entries rarely need cross-table relationships, so relational constraints are skipped, and workloads seldom need indefinite retention, which cuts storage and speeds queries. Specialized compression such as delta encoding or Gorilla compression, temporal indexing, and lifecycle management that drops whole old partitions in bulk exploit that uniformity.

sysd-blocks-043.title: Concurrency control: keeping simultaneous transactions correct
sysd-blocks-043.text: Running transactions at the same time is safe only if something keeps them from corrupting one another. Concurrency control is the set of mechanisms in a DBMS that handle isolation and guarantee the correctness of concurrent transactions. It constrains the timing of data access operations to orders that have the serializability and recoverability properties, which typically reduces performance. Serializability is often compromised for better performance when correctness allows, but recoverability cannot be, because that typically violates database integrity. The most common method, {{ref:sysd-blocks-165}}, works through locks. A transaction must first acquire a lock on an object, and that may be blocked while another transaction holds one.

sysd-blocks-171.title: ETL and ELT: two ways to fill a warehouse
sysd-blocks-171.text: Two workflows load a data warehouse, and they differ in where the transformation happens. In ETL, a staging layer holds raw data extracted from each source, and an integration layer transforms it, often into an operational data store. The integrated data then moves into the warehouse database, arranged into dimensions, facts and aggregate facts, and an access layer helps users retrieve it. ETL is inherently a batch process in most implementations. ELT drops the separate transformation tool. Data is extracted from heterogeneous sources and loaded straight into a staging area inside the warehouse, where all transformations run before landing in target tables.

sysd-blocks-173.title: Multi-model database: several models, one backend
sysd-blocks-173.text: Most DBMSs are organized around one data model. A multi-model database stores, indexes and queries data in more than one, such as document, graph, relational and key-value, against a single, integrated backend. It answers the weakness of polyglot persistence, whose several products bring operational complexity and no consistency across stores. Reported advantages include ingesting varied formats such as CSV and JSON without extra effort, and one query language, such as AQL or SQL/JSON, over related data. Architectures differ. Some engines support models such as documents and graphs natively, while others layer each model over an engine such as a key-value store.

sysd-blocks-163.title: NewSQL: SQL with the scale of NoSQL
sysd-blocks-163.text: Financial and order-processing systems outgrew conventional relational databases yet needed transactional guarantees that NoSQL could not give. NewSQL tries to reconcile the two. It is a class of relational database systems that seek the online scale of NoSQL while keeping ACID guarantees. The relational model and SQL remain the primary interface. Typical applications have heavy OLTP volumes of short-lived transactions that touch little data. Systems fall into three groups. Some are shared-nothing clusters, where each node manages a subset of the data. Some put optimized storage behind a SQL interface. Others shard transparently across nodes that agree through {{ref:sysd-scale-008}}.

sysd-blocks-063.title: N+1 query problem: one query plus N more
sysd-blocks-063.text: One query fetches a list, and then N more fetch details that the first query could have returned. That is the N+1 query problem. The data access layer executes N additional SQL statements to fetch data that the primary query could have retrieved. The larger N is, the more queries run and the larger the performance impact. It is commonly seen in ORM tools and in {{ref:sysd-msg-004}}. The fix is to optimize the SQL query, or to use a dataloader that batches consecutive requests into a single data request.

sysd-blocks-065.title: Transaction states: from active to terminated
sysd-blocks-065.text: A transaction starts in the active state, where it is being executed. When it executes its final operation it is partially committed, and when all operations succeed it is committed and its effects are permanently established. If any check by the recovery system fails, it is failed and cannot proceed. The recovery manager then rolls back all its writes, restoring the database to its earlier state, and the transaction is aborted. The recovery module can restart or kill it. After a commit, or with no rollback, the system is consistent and ready for a new transaction, and the old one is terminated.

sysd-blocks-049.title: Database schema: the shape of the data
sysd-blocks-049.text: A schema defines the shape of a data structure, specifying what kinds of data can go where. It can be strictly enforced across the entire database, loosely enforced on part of it, or not exist at all. A table has columns like a spreadsheet, from two to a hundred or more, each holding values of one type, with one value per row. A table can hold thousands or millions of rows. In SQL every record conforms to a fixed schema, chosen before data entry and changed only through migrations. In NoSQL the schema is dynamic and fields can be added on the fly.

sysd-blocks-054.title: Multiversion concurrency control: readers never wait for writers
sysd-blocks-054.text: Locks make readers wait for writers, which causes contention, especially between long read transactions and update transactions. Multiversion concurrency control avoids that by keeping multiple copies of each data item. An update creates a newer version instead of overwriting. Each user therefore sees a snapshot of the database at one instant, and a writer's changes stay invisible to others until it commits. The version a transaction sees depends on the isolation level, and the most common pairing is {{ref:sysd-blocks-166}}, where a transaction observes the data as of when it started. Readers pick the version by timestamp or transaction ID. Reads and writes are isolated without locks, so writers do not block readers, though some databases such as Oracle still use locks. Obsolete versions need cleanup. PostgreSQL's VACUUM FREEZE sweeps and rewrites the table periodically. Other systems keep the latest version plus an undo log, which can run out of space and abort transactions. The cost is storing multiple versions. The benefit is that reads are never blocked, which matters for read-heavy workloads.

sysd-blocks-165.title: Two-phase locking: acquire everything, then release
sysd-blocks-165.text: A transaction never acquires a lock after releasing one. That single rule is two-phase locking, a pessimistic concurrency control method that guarantees conflict-serializability by making each transaction acquire all its locks before releasing any. Locks are acquired in an expanding phase with none released, then released in a shrinking phase with none acquired, and schedules obeying this are serializable. The basic protocol uses shared (read) and exclusive (write) locks. Reading needs a read or write lock, writing needs a write lock, and several locks on one object may coexist only if none is a write lock. Because locks block, the protocol can deadlock when two or more transactions block each other. Strict 2PL releases write locks only after the transaction commits or aborts. Strong strict 2PL also holds read locks until the end, and most commercial database systems use it. Conservative 2PL takes every lock before execution, so a lock holder never blocks. It over-locks under light contention and needs declared read and write sets, so it is rarely used. Do not confuse any of this with {{ref:sysd-scale-002}}.

sysd-blocks-177.title: PostgreSQL isolation levels: four names, three behaviors
sysd-blocks-177.text:
PostgreSQL accepts the four standard levels, covered in {{ref:sysd-blocks-041}}, but implements only three distinct ones, all built on {{ref:sysd-blocks-054}}. Read Uncommitted behaves like Read Committed, the only sensible mapping onto its architecture.

Read Committed is the default. A SELECT sees only data committed before the query began, so two successive SELECTs in one transaction can see different data if others commit between them. It is fine for simple cases such as transferring $100 between accounts. It is unsuitable for complex search conditions, where one command can see an inconsistent snapshot.

Repeatable Read sees only data committed before the transaction began. That is stronger than the standard requires. It prevents every phenomenon, phantom reads included, except anomalies whose committed results match no one-at-a-time ordering of the transactions. A Repeatable Read transaction that tries to modify a row changed by a concurrent committed transaction is rolled back with an error. Applications must then retry the whole transaction. The view is stable but not necessarily consistent with a serial execution, so business rules may need explicit locks.

sysd-blocks-166.title: Snapshot isolation: a private snapshot for each transaction
sysd-blocks-166.text:
Oracle, and PostgreSQL before 9.1, call snapshot isolation their serializable mode, even though it is not serializable. The naming is confusing, so users must know the difference to avoid anomalous behavior.

Snapshot isolation guarantees that all reads in a transaction see a consistent snapshot of the database. The transaction commits only if its updates do not conflict with concurrent updates made since that snapshot. It works on a personal snapshot taken when it starts, and a write-write conflict aborts it if the values it updated have been changed externally since. It is usually implemented within multiversion concurrency control, so the transaction need only store its list of updates, which is scanned for conflicts before commit.

Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server and MongoDB, among others, adopted it. It performs better than serializability while still avoiding most, but not all, of the anomalies serializability avoids. It shows none of the anomalies the ANSI SQL-92 standard prohibited, yet it permits others such as {{ref:sysd-blocks-167}}. PostgreSQL implements Repeatable Read with it, so successive SELECTs see the same data.

sysd-blocks-041.title: Isolation levels: trading protection for concurrency
sysd-blocks-041.text:
A database may run your transaction at a stronger level than the one you asked for, and the standard allows it. Isolation levels are settings that control how much locking a transaction does when selecting data, trading protection from concurrency effects against concurrency. Each is stronger than those below it, so a request for Read committed may be performed as Repeatable read.

SERIALIZABLE guarantees the same effect as some serial execution, in which each transaction runs to completion before the next begins. Lock-based systems hold read and write locks to the end and take range locks for ranged SELECTs. Without locks, a serializable system detects write collisions among concurrent transactions and lets only one of them commit. REPEATABLE READ keeps read and write locks until the end of the transaction but manages no range locks. Phantom reads can therefore occur, and {{ref:sysd-blocks-167}} is possible in some systems. READ COMMITTED guarantees that any data read was committed when read, but promises nothing if the read is repeated. READ UNCOMMITTED allows dirty reads, so one transaction may see not-yet-committed changes made by others.

The default level varies quite widely between DBMSs, and most transactional databases let the user set any level. The ANSI definitions, based on three read phenomena, have been criticized as ambiguous and as not reflecting the isolation many databases actually provide.

sysd-blocks-042.title: Read phenomena: dirty, non-repeatable and phantom reads
sysd-blocks-042.text:
The SQL-92 standard names three read phenomena that can occur when a transaction retrieves data another transaction might have updated. A dirty read occurs when a transaction retrieves a row that another transaction has updated but not yet committed. If that update is rolled back, the first transaction's view of the row is wrong. A non-repeatable read occurs when a transaction retrieves a row twice and another transaction commits an update to that row in between. A phantom read occurs when a transaction retrieves a set of rows twice and another transaction commits an insert or removal in that set in between.

Each phenomenon belongs to particular levels. Dirty reads occur only at READ UNCOMMITTED, non-repeatable reads at READ UNCOMMITTED and READ COMMITTED, and phantom reads at every level except SERIALIZABLE.

The standard only specifies which phenomena must not occur at each level, so a database may give stronger guarantees. PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read, for example, allows no phantom reads. Being free of all three is necessary but not sufficient for a serializable schedule. A fourth phenomenon shows why: a group of transactions whose committed result is inconsistent with every possible ordering of running them one at a time. Another is {{ref:sysd-blocks-167}}, in which two writers who each read the same columns both update them, leaving data that mixes the two transactions.

sysd-blocks-167.title: Write skew: the anomaly snapshot isolation allows
sysd-blocks-167.text:
A bank lets either of two accounts run a deficit as long as their total stays at or above zero. Two concurrent $200 withdrawals each check against their own snapshot, both commit, and the total ends at -$200. That is write skew: two concurrent transactions read an overlapping data set, make disjoint updates and both commit, unaware of each other. Under serializability it is impossible, because one of the two transactions would have to occur first and be visible to the other. Snapshot isolation permits it.

The fix is to force a write-write conflict. One way is a conflict table that both transactions update. Another is promoting a read to a write, such as Oracle's SELECT FOR UPDATE. The workarounds have costs. A table that materializes the constraint violates normal form, promotion is not always possible, and snapshot isolation leaves the user to maintain non-trivial constraints.

Serializable Snapshot Isolation removes the workarounds. It detects and aborts dangerous triplets of concurrent transactions, as Cahill and colleagues showed in 2008, at the cost of more aborts. PostgreSQL 9.1 adopted it.

reviews.choosing-a-database: A database is an organized collection of data, and the relational kind keeps it in tables of rows and columns, linked by keys, queried with SQL and protected by ACID transactions. NoSQL databases, in key-value, document, wide-column and graph form, give up some of that for horizontal scaling and looser BASE guarantees. Around the transaction grew a ladder of isolation levels, with locking and multiversion methods to enforce them and write skew to show what a level can still miss. Workloads then pull the choices apart again, from OLTP systems feeding warehouses to specialized stores for text, vectors, locations and time series. Singh's advice runs through all of it: weigh the requirements, because SQL against NoSQL and ACID against BASE are trade-offs, not contests.
